Content:
When solving an inhomogeneous BVP, it is important to know whether the boundary conditions determine a unique solution. In this topic, we will learn how the solution behavior of an inhomogeneous BVP depends on the corresponding homogeneous BVP.

Content:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)
[MATH: y''(x) + P(x)y'(x) + Q(x)y(x) = f(x), \qquad a \le x \le b]
with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions
[MATH: \alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2.]

Content:
Let the associated homogeneous BVP be
[MATH: y''(x) + P(x)y'(x) + Q(x)y(x) = 0, \qquad a \le x \le b]
with the boundary conditions
[MATH: \alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = 0, \qquad
\alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = 0.]

Content:
Then we have the following:

Content:
> The inhomogeneous BVP has a unique solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution [MATH: y \equiv 0.]

Content:
We interpret this as follows:

Content:
- If the homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution [MATH: y \equiv 0,] then the inhomogeneous BVP has a unique solution.
- If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous BVP either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

Content:
In particular, if the inhomogeneous BVP has one solution [MATH: y_p] and the homogeneous BVP has a nontrivial solution [MATH: y_c,] then
[MATH: y = c\,y_c + y_p]
is a solution for every [MATH: c\in\mathbb R.] Therefore, the inhomogeneous BVP has infinitely many solutions.

Content:
In the next slide, we'll show how to use this criterion if the general solution of the homogeneous BVP is known.

sections.normalized_html:
Suppose we have the second-order inhomogeneous boundary value problem (BVP)

[MATH: y''(x) + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = f(x), \qquad a \leq x \leq b]

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

[MATH: \alpha_1 y(a) + \beta_1 y'(a) = \gamma_1, \qquad \alpha_2 y(b) + \beta_2 y'(b) = \gamma_2] where [MATH: P, Q,] and [MATH: f] are continuous on [MATH: [a,b],] and [MATH: \alpha_i] and [MATH: \beta_i] are real constants such that [MATH: (\alpha_i, \beta_i) \neq (0,0).]

The inhomogeneous BVP has at most one solution if and only if the associated homogeneous BVP has only the trivial solution [MATH: y \equiv 0.] Specifically:

  • If the homogeneous BVP has the unique solution [MATH: y \equiv 0,] then the inhomogeneous problem either has no solution or a unique solution.

  • If the homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, then the inhomogeneous problem either has infinitely many solutions or no solution.

To classify the solutions of the corresponding homogeneous BVP, we define the matrix [MATH: A] as

[MATH: [α_{1}y_{1}(a) + β_{1}y_{1}^{′}(a)|α_{1}y_{2}(a) + β_{1}y_{2}^{′}(a); α_{2}y_{1}(b) + β_{2}y_{1}^{′}(b)|α_{2}y_{2}(b) + β_{2}y_{2}^{′}(b)]]

The homogeneous BVP has a unique, trivial solution [MATH: y \equiv 0] if and only if [MATH: \det(A) \neq 0.] In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the homogeneous BVP has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting [MATH: \alpha_i = 0, \beta_i = 1, a = 0,] and [MATH: b = \pi,] the matrix [MATH: A] reduces to

[MATH: [y_{1}^{′}(0)|y_{2}^{′}(0); y_{1}^{′}(π)|y_{2}^{′}(π)]]

To find the fundamental solutions, we set [MATH: y = e^{m x}.] The auxiliary equation is [MATH: m^{2} + 16|= 0.] So, we have [MATH: m = \pm 4\textrm i.] So, the fundamental solutions are [MATH: y_1(x) = \cos 4x, \qquad y_2(x) = \sin 4x.] Differentiating, we have [MATH: y_1'(x) = -4\sin 4x, \qquad y_2'(x) = 4\cos 4x.]

Therefore, the matrix [MATH: A] is [MATH: A|= [− 4\sin (4 ⋅ 0)|4\cos (4 ⋅ 0); − 4\sin (4 ⋅ π)|4\cos (4 ⋅ π)]; = [0|4; 0|4]]

and we have [MATH: |det(A)||=|0 ⋅ 4 − 4 ⋅ 0|; = 0.]

Since [MATH: \det(A) = 0,] the corresponding homogeneous BVP [MATH: \textrm{has infinitely many solutions}.]

Therefore, since the corresponding homogeneous BVP has (infinitely many) nontrivial solutions, our inhomogeneous BVP [MATH: \textrm{has infinitely many solutions or no solution}.]
